Florence, March. Dr Ferraris has finally come to the trattoria for a ribollita. He learns that on Monday the cooperative has to negotiate with the bursar of the diocese of Siena over the restoration of don Paolo's Madonna. He offers to teach Matei and Karl.
How much did you ask the diocese for?
Forty-eight thousand euros. They're offering thirty thousand.
And what's the figure you can't go below?
Thirty-eight thousand. Below that, we'd be working at a loss.
Good. First rule: never say that figure. Second rule: don't negotiate the price, negotiate the conditions.
Meaning: "We could meet you halfway on the price, provided the payment is in three instalments." Give something, but ask for something in exchange.
And if the monsignor says: "Thirty thousand, not a cent more"?
Then you ask him what the diocese really wants. Nobody wants only a low price. Everyone wants something else.
And if we don't reach an agreement?
You stand up, say thank you and leave. Unless you're afraid of losing the job. But they need you as much as you need them.
I'll add a column to the handbook: "How to negotiate".

Dr Ferraris arrived in via Maggio one Saturday in March, unannounced, at eight in the evening. He was a man of about sixty, tall, with very short grey hair and a blue coat that looked as if it cost as much as the analysis machine. In his hand he had a box of sweets from Bergamo, the yellow ones with little sugar birds on top. He stopped at the trattoria door, looked at the brass plaque, the 1966 plaque, the checked tablecloths, and asked Graziella whether the invitation for a ribollita was still valid. Graziella, who didn't know who he was, replied that in that trattoria the ribollita was valid for anyone who came in hungry and well-mannered. Ferraris said he had both, and sat down.

Matei recognised him only after ten minutes, when Karl, who waited on tables on Saturdays to earn a bit extra, came back into the kitchen very pale and whispered: "The Milan group is at table six." Matei came out of the kitchen with his apron still on. Ferraris stood up, shook his hand and told him the ribollita was the best he had ever eaten, and that he wasn't saying it out of politeness, because in his job he never said anything out of politeness. Then he asked to see Ernesto's diary. Matei went to fetch it from the workshop. Ferraris leafed through it for half an hour, in silence, with his glasses on the tip of his nose, lingering over the pages from 1946 and 1966. When he gave it back, his eyes were moist. "My grandfather kept a notebook just like this," he said. "We lost it in a house move. I've never forgiven myself."

It was during coffee that Ferraris noticed the sheet on the next table. It was the quote for the diocese of Siena, the one for the complete restoration of don Paolo's Madonna, which Matei and Karl had prepared that afternoon and left there to reread. Ferraris asked permission, took it and read it carefully, the way a doctor reads an X-ray. "Forty-eight thousand euros," he said. "Well done. Precise. Honest. And how much are they offering you?" Matei explained that the diocese's bursar, Monsignor Cappelli, had already replied by email: thirty thousand, not a cent more. The decisive meeting was set for the following Monday, at ten, at the curia in Siena. Ferraris took off his glasses. "Cappelli," he repeated slowly. "God's notary. I know him by reputation. He's the toughest negotiator in Tuscany."

Graziella, hearing the word "negotiator", sat down at the table with a glass of wine, as she did when a conversation became interesting. Ferraris explained to her that Monsignor Cappelli had been the diocese's bursar for forty years, and that every restorer, architect and builder in the province of Siena had a story about him. People said he had a calculator older than himself, and that in his whole career he had never accepted anyone's first offer. People also said he was the most honest man in the curia, and that this was why the bishops had kept him there for forty years. "With someone like that," Ferraris concluded, "if you go on Monday with just your quote, you'll come home with thirty thousand euros and a headache." Matei and Karl looked at each other. Then Karl took out his notebook.

What followed was, according to Pietro, the strangest lesson ever held in the trattoria in via Maggio, and there had been quite a few. Ferraris, the sales director who had wanted to buy the cooperative, taught the cooperative how to defend itself from someone like him. First rule: know the figure below which you cannot go, and never say it. Matei did the sums with Karl on a paper napkin: materials, analyses, four months of work for three people, the workshop rent, the loan instalment. Below thirty-eight thousand euros they would be working at a loss. "Good," said Ferraris. "Thirty-eight thousand. Now forget it. That number doesn't exist. If you say it, the monsignor will pay you exactly thirty-eight thousand euros and you'll be happy to have lost."

Second rule: don't negotiate the price, negotiate the conditions. "The price is a number," Ferraris explained, drawing a line on the napkin. "If you negotiate only the number, one wins and the other loses. But a negotiation has many things inside it: deadlines, payments, guarantees, extra work. Each one is a coin. You give one coin and ask for another in exchange." And he showed them how to say it: "We could meet you halfway on the price, provided the payment is divided into three instalments." "We are willing to revise the quote, on condition that the deadlines are longer." "That's fine, as long as the contract also provides for…" Karl wrote everything down. In a new column of the handbook, which that evening he titled "How to negotiate", he drew a small pair of scales next to each formula.

The third rule was discovered by Pietro, who had been listening to everything from the homework table, pretending to do his maths exercises. He raised his hand, as at school, and asked: "But what does the diocese really want? It can't just want to spend little. Otherwise it wouldn't have the Madonna restored." Ferraris turned to him with an expression nobody had seen on him yet: a real smile. "That," he said, "is the most important question of the whole evening. And the youngest person asked it. As always." Then he explained that in every negotiation the other side wants something it doesn't say. Whoever discovers what has already won half the game. "The price is what the monsignor says," he concluded. "But you have to discover what the monsignor wants."

On Sunday morning Karl phoned don Paolo. He apologised for the disturbance on the Lord's day, with three different formulas, until the old priest laughingly told him to get to the point. Karl asked him, very delicately, why the diocese wanted to restore that particular Madonna. Don Paolo was silent for a long time. Then he explained that the church of San Leonardo now had only forty parishioners, almost all over seventy. The young people had gone to the city. On Sundays, at Mass, there were more candles than people. The bishop feared that, once don Paolo died, the church would be closed, like so many other country churches. "The bishop doesn't want a restored painting," said don Paolo. "He wants a living church. But the monsignor will never tell you that. He only talks about numbers."

On Monday morning three of them set off for Siena: Matei, Chiara and Karl, in Giulia's old car, with the quote in a folder and the laminated handbook in a pocket. Nobody spoke for the whole journey. The curia was a grey palazzo behind the cathedral, with stone stairs worn by centuries of priests and suppliers. Monsignor Cappelli received them in a tiny office, full of files, with a wooden crucifix on the wall and a gigantic calculator on the desk, its keys worn. He was seventy-nine, with thick glasses and a thin, very kind voice. He had them sit down, offered them a glass of water, asked about their journey. Then he opened the quote, looked at it for five seconds and closed it. "The diocese can offer thirty thousand euros," he said gently. "Not a cent more."

Matei replied as they had rehearsed the evening before. "We fully understand the diocese's needs, Monsignor. However, with this sum I'm afraid we would not be able to guarantee the quality the work deserves, at least on these terms." Monsignor Cappelli nodded, as if he had heard that sentence a thousand times. "Everyone says that," he replied, with the same gentleness. Then Chiara explained the work: the analyses, the cleaning, the consolidation of the wood, the fourteenth-century pigment to be protected, the months needed. She spoke for ten minutes, with passion and precision. The monsignor listened to everything without interrupting, taking notes in pencil. At the end he typed something on the gigantic calculator, looked at the result and said: "Thirty-five thousand. It is our final offer." A heavy silence fell in the office.

It was Karl who broke the silence. He didn't look at the handbook. He leaned forward a little and said: "Monsignor, may I make you a proposal that isn't about the price?" Cappelli raised an eyebrow. "We are willing to do the restoration not in the workshop, in Florence, but in the church itself, as an open worksite. On Saturdays anyone could come and watch the work: the parishioners, the schools in the nearby villages, passing tourists. Pietro, a boy who works with us, could act as a guide, as he already does in Florence. Davide, another boy, could draw the restoration for a little book. And a journalist we know would write an article every month." He paused, as Bellini had taught Pietro. "For four months, the church of San Leonardo would be the most visited church in the province."

Monsignor Cappelli didn't answer at once. He took off his glasses, cleaned them slowly with a handkerchief, put them back on. Matei and Chiara were holding their breath. Karl, who had just made a proposal nobody had discussed with him, suddenly realised what he had done and blushed to the ears. "And in exchange?" the monsignor asked at last. "In exchange," replied Karl, in a voice more confident than he felt, "forty-two thousand euros. Because an open worksite costs more: scaffolding in the church, insurance, the daily trip from Florence." The monsignor took his pencil and wrote something. "And who guarantees that people will come?" he asked. "Nobody, Monsignor," admitted Karl. "But in Florence, on Saturdays, eighty people come to our workshop. And the workshop is in a narrow street, with no parking."

For the first time, Monsignor Cappelli smiled. It was a tiny smile, barely a movement at the corner of his mouth, but Chiara later swore she had seen it. The monsignor typed on the calculator again, for a long time, as if he were calculating the orbit of a planet. Then he said: "Thirty-eight thousand. As long as the cooperative also restores the small crucifix in the sacristy, which has been falling to pieces for twenty years. At no extra cost." Karl looked at Matei. It was exactly the figure below which they could not go. Matei felt his heart pounding: thirty-eight thousand euros plus a crucifix meant working at a loss. But he remembered Ferraris's second rule. Not the price, the conditions. "We could accept the crucifix, Monsignor," he said slowly, "on condition that the payment is divided into three instalments, and that the first arrives before the work begins."

"Acceptable," said the monsignor. "And then?" Chiara understood it was time to split the difference. "And then forty thousand," she said. "Halfway between your figure and Karl's. And the right to use the photographs of the restoration for our website and for an exhibition, in Florence, at the end of the work." The monsignor thought about it. He looked at the wooden crucifix on the wall, as if asking it for advice. Then he said a sentence none of them expected: "Unless you prefer forty-one thousand without the exhibition." Matei, Chiara and Karl looked at each other, confused. Was the monsignor raising the price himself? Cappelli adjusted his glasses. "An exhibition in Florence about our church," he explained gently, "is worth more than a thousand euros to the diocese. I don't give it away so easily."

It took them a moment to understand. The monsignor didn't want to spend less: he wanted the exhibition. He wanted people in Florence to talk about his forgotten church. It was what the bishop really wanted, what don Paolo had said on the phone: a living church. Matei smiled. "Forty thousand with the exhibition, Monsignor," he said. "Deal." Cappelli held out his hand across the desk, and the handshake was surprisingly strong for a man of seventy-nine. "Deal," he repeated. "Let's put it in writing. Send me a confirmation email by this evening." Then he added, turning to Karl: "And you write it, young man. Don Paolo let me read your first letter. I want to see whether the second is just as good."

As they were getting up to leave, the monsignor opened a drawer of his desk and took out an old yellowed envelope. "One last thing," he said. "You come from the workshop in via Maggio, don't you? Bellini's?" Matei nodded, surprised. The monsignor handed him the envelope. Inside was a typewritten letter from 1972, with Ernesto Bellini's signature. It was the quote for the restoration of a crucifix in a church near Montalcino. "In 1972 I was a young priest," the monsignor recounted, "and secretary to the old bursar. Ernesto came here, to this office, and negotiated for two hours. In the end he lowered the price, but he got to do the restoration in the church, in front of the farmers. He told me a sentence I have never forgotten." He paused. "'Not the price, Monsignor. The conditions.'"

On the way back, in Giulia's old car, nobody managed to keep quiet. Chiara imitated the monsignor's voice: "Thirty thousand. Not a cent more." Matei laughed at the wheel. Karl, in the back seat, wrote the confirmation email on his phone, deleted it and rewrote it. In the end he read it aloud: "Most Reverend Monsignor, with reference to today's cordial meeting, we are pleased to confirm the agreement reached, on the following terms…" Then came the list: forty thousand euros in three instalments, the sacristy crucifix, the open worksite on Saturdays, the exhibition in Florence. Chiara listened to the end and said it was perfect. Matei said only one thing was missing. "What?" asked Karl, worried. "A thank-you to Ernesto," replied Matei. "But that isn't written in emails."

That evening Matei phoned Ferraris, in Milan, and told him everything, from the first offer to the 1972 envelope. Ferraris listened in silence. When Matei got to the point where Karl had proposed forty-two thousand euros, Ferraris burst out laughing so loudly that Matei had to hold the phone away from his ear. "You did exactly the opposite of what I taught you," he said when he could speak. "I told you to come down slowly from your price. And you raised the price. In front of God's notary." Then he became serious. "But you did the most important thing. You discovered what he really wanted. In thirty years of negotiations, I've managed that maybe ten times." Before hanging up, he added that in May he would be back in Tuscany, and that he wanted to see the open worksite. "As a paying visitor," he specified. "Non-negotiable."

At the trattoria the celebrations went on until late. Graziella brought out the Sunday cake even though it was Monday, and when Karl explained Ferraris's three rules to her, she shrugged. "Big discovery," she said. "I've been negotiating every morning for fifty years. With the fishmonger, with the baker, with the greengrocer at the Santo Spirito market. I never discuss the price. I discuss the conditions: the freshest fish, yesterday's bread thrown in for the ribollita, courgettes with their flowers." She paused, the knife held above the cake. "And I always know what the greengrocer really wants. He wants someone to ask him about his grandchildren." Everyone laughed. Karl opened the handbook and, in the column "How to negotiate", under Ferraris's formulas, added in small letters: "Rule four (Graziella): ask about the grandchildren."

Before going to bed, Pietro wrote in the black notebook. He stuck in the paper napkin with Matei's sums, which he had rescued from the rubbish, and below it copied Ernesto's sentence, the one the monsignor had kept in a drawer for more than fifty years. Then he thought for a long time and wrote his conclusions, numbered, the way Ferraris did. "One: whoever asks the right question wins half the game. Two: the price is what someone says, but the truth is what they want. Three: the right sentences last longer than people. Ernesto died many years ago, but today he won a negotiation in Siena." He reread the third conclusion, and it seemed the truest. Then, below, he added a fourth line, in small letters, for himself: "Four: always ask about the grandchildren."
